papers.title_en: Dephasing-Induced Melting of Crystalline Spectral Form Factors
papers.abstract_en: Long-range spectral order can be probed using spectral form factors, where it manifests itself as sharp Bragg peaks at integer multiples of the Heisenberg time in nearly crystalline spectra. We examine how energy dephasing in open systems affects this spectral order and how to control it. We find that Bragg peaks fade algebraically with revival order and dephasing strength, $K_{\rm Bragg}(p)\propto(γp)^{-1/2}$, within an extensive intermediate regime, and persist up to the lifetime of nearest-neighbor coherences despite an extreme decoherence rate. Our results establish the spectral form factor as a probe of spectral order in open quantum systems and identify temporal correlations in spectral fluctuations as a means of controlling it.

papers.title_en: First demonstration of long-distance electron drift in liquid xenon with the Xenoscope time projection chamber
papers.abstract_en: Xenoscope is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated at the University of Zurich to investigate electron transport over distances relevant to the next-generation XLZD (XENON-LUX-ZEPLIN-DARWIN) observatory. We demonstrate electron drift over $2.6$ m in liquid xenon using cosmic-muon-induced ionization signals. External muon tagging provides a timing reference for charge produced at known depths, while the endpoint of the average electroluminescence waveform probes transport over the full drift length. We measure electron drift velocities of $(1.320 \pm 0.006)$ mm/$μ$s at $(80.92 \pm 0.36)$ V/cm and $(1.436 \pm 0.001)$ mm/$μ$s at $(96.00 \pm 0.42)$ V/cm. These results establish detectable charge transport over meter-scale distances and provide an experimental benchmark for the development of future large liquid-xenon time projection chambers.

papers.title_en: A regularization-independent Information Criterion for correlated data
papers.abstract_en: We generalize the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to allow model and data subset selection when regularized fits are performed on correlated data. While the standard generalization to regularized fits is inherently dependent on the type of regularization applied to the data covariance matrix, our definition, the RIAIC, is, on average, regularization-independent. The regularization-independence is achieved by defining the new Information Criterion as an estimator of the model-dependent contribution to the correlated Kullback--Leibler divergence. The Bayesian extension is derived as well. We test the new criterion on lattice QCD data by performing regularized fits and show that it reproduces the selection properties of the standard correlated AIC, with fluctuations which are compatible with the expected statistical uncertainties. These results enable the application of subset and model selection techniques to cases where regularizations are applied to the covariance matrix of the fitted dataset.

papers.title_en: Frequency tuning capability of self-powered piezoelectric tuned mass dampers
papers.abstract_en: Tuned mass dampers suffer from frequency shift sensitivity. This paper investigates the use of tunable piezoelectric tuned mass dampers (PE-TMD) by studying their behavior with tunable resistive and capacitive loads to adapt their resonant frequency. An analytical model is developed to assess the influence of key dimensionless parameters-electromechanical coupling coefficient, mass ratio, and quality factoron vibration attenuation, frequency tuning capability, and energy harvesting. The study reveals trade-offs between attenuation, tunability, and energy harvesting. It provides design guidelines for autonomous PE-TMDs and identifies key challenges for their practical implementation, including the interest of high coupling coefficients, whose the implication is limited is with growing mass ratio. Notably, it highlights the necessity of high coupling coefficient, the influence of which on frequency tuning is limited as the mass ratio grows.
publication_info: International Conference on Noise and Vibration Engineering - ISMA 2026, Sep 2026, Leuven, Belgium, publication

papers.title_en: Deploying QKD on the fiber links of the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden
papers.abstract_en: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is being deployed across Europe to evaluate its performance and practicality in real-world scenarios. When preparing this deployment, it is important to survey the properties of the fiber links that will be used for the quantum channel, cross-checking them with those of QKD devices, to ensure compatibility and optimal performance. We report here our studies from the Swedish chapter of this endeavor, the National Quantum Communication Infrastructure in Sweden. We focus on procedures to characterize the links and evaluate their suitability for QKD. We relate measurable properties to the key factors that affect the secret key rate using a simplified model that aims at the essence of QKD performance. Finally, we confirm the feasibility of QKD on one of our links by reporting a one-month long successful test.

papers.title_en: Electroweak Parton Distribution Functions for Future Lepton Colliders
papers.abstract_en: At future high-energy colliders, such as a multi-TeV muon collider or the high-energy stages of an $e^+e^-$ linear collider, collinear radiation of electroweak gauge bosons becomes a dominant phenomenon. In this regime, many key processes are primarily initiated by photons and gauge bosons originating from lepton splittings. Electroweak Parton Distribution Functions (EW PDFs) provide an appropriate framework to describe these interactions by resumming large collinear logarithms arising from all possible Standard Model splittings, thereby enabling a partonic interpretation of the hard scattering. The formalism is particularly suitable for studying new physics beyond the Standard Model in the electroweak sector at higher scales. In this paper, we present the implementation of the EW PDF formalism within the Monte Carlo event generator \texttt{Whizard}. We demonstrate several applications of this framework and analyze its interplay with full fixed-order calculations as well as the purely kinematic Effective Weak Boson Approximation. We highlight scenarios where the EW PDF approach is especially useful for phenomenology and physics-potential studies for future lepton colliders. The EW PDF formalism is a vital step towards the ``electroweak jet regime'' where electroweak particles behave similarly to QCD jets.

papers.title_en: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
papers.abstract_en: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.

papers.title_en: FORM 5.0 and further developments
papers.abstract_en: In these proceedings we review the features of the recently-released version 5.0 of the FORM computer algebra system, which is one of the core software packages for the large-scale symbolic manipulations required by calculations in theoretical high-energy physics. We also discuss developments since the release of version 5.0, focussing in particular on recent performance improvements.

papers.title_en: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
papers.abstract_en: In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers. Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.

papers.title_en: A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework
papers.abstract_en: We give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. If a partial Boolean function $f$ is defined on a $δ$-fraction of all $n$-bit strings and have quantum query complexity $Q(f)$, then, for every $0<ε<1$, a deterministic algorithm computes $f$ correctly on at least a $1-ε$ fraction of its domain using $O( Q(f)^6 / (εδ)^2)$ queries. Our proof uses the completion framework and establishes a more general bound in terms of the classical adversary measure. The only result we use from Turturean's recent proof is a special case of his certificate inequality, for which we provide a self-contained proof. We also derive the stronger variant of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, from our main result in the appendix.

papers.title_en: Quantum Robustness via Sandwiched Rényi Divergences
papers.abstract_en: If a quantum state is known only approximately, how much can the expectation of an observable change? We answer with the worst-case expectation over all states within a sandwiched Rényi divergence budget of a reference state, for every order $α\in [1/2,\infty]$. Convex duality gives this value as a one-dimensional optimization over a sandwiched Schatten norm, running from a fidelity risk at $α= 1/2$, through the entropic risk at $α= 1$, to a quantum conditional value-at-risk at $α= \infty$. The main result is a classicalization theorem: the quantum problem coincides with the classical one for a probability measure $ω_α$ on the spectral interval of the observable, constructed from Heinävaara's tracial joint spectral measure and given by Stahl's theorem at $α= 1$. The Hoeffding, Bernstein and Markov--Krein bounds of classical probability thereby apply to the quantum problem, and yield Pinsker-type inequalities with Bernstein-type refinements. The measure $ω_α$ is the Born measure only at $α= 1/2$; for $α> 1/2$, noncommutativity of the observable with the state strictly lowers its variance below the Born variance, and with it every variance-sensitive bound: a quantum deflation.

papers.title_en: Polynomial-Space Quantum Algorithms from Classical Branching: Colouring, Domination and Monotone Local Search
papers.abstract_en: We give quantum algorithms for exponential-time problems on $n$ vertices or elements, with bounded error, polynomial space and no quantum random access memory. Our results are these. (1) 4-Colouring in quantum time $O(1.3032^n)$, from a polynomial-space branching algorithm with polynomial-space terminal algorithms; with the branching algorithm alone, $O(1.3100^n)$. The previous best bound in this model, to our knowledge, is $O(1.3231^n)$. (2) $k$-Colouring below the previous best bound for $k \in \{5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11\}$ and $13 \le k \le 18$, from $O(1.4518^n)$ for $k = 5$ to $O(1.9233^n)$ for $k = 18$. (3) Dominating Set in $O(1.2235^n)$, against the previous $O(2^{n/2})$, Independent Dominating Set in $O(1.1583^n)$, and Edge Dominating Set and Minimum Maximal Matching in $O(1.1501^n)$. (4) A quantum form of monotone local search: if the extension problem has a backtracking tree with $c^k$ nodes up to polynomial factors, the problem is solved in quantum time $(2 - 1/c)^{n/2}$ up to polynomial factors. This gives Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3081^n)$, Subset and Group Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3229^n)$, Cluster Vertex Deletion in $O(1.2033^n)$, 3-Hitting Set in $O(1.2405^n)$, Proper Interval Vertex Deletion in $O(1.3541^n)$, Multicut on Trees in $O(1.1647^n)$ and Min-Ones $d$-SAT in $O^*((2-1/d)^{n/2})$. (5) Quantum exponential-time approximations below the quantum exact bounds, such as a 1.1-approximation for Vertex Cover in $O(1.0555^n)$ and for Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.2161^n)$. The colouring exponents for $k \ge 6$ come from an evaluation of a known reduction recursion, computed in floating point with a margin.

papers.title_en: $\mathsf{EQP}\subseteq\mathsf{IP}$ Does Not Relativize
papers.abstract_en: We construct a recursive oracle $O$ and a unary language $L\in\mathsf{EQP}^O\setminus(\mathsf{IP}^O\cup\mathsf{PH}^O)$, strengthening the $\mathsf{BQP}$ versus $\mathsf{IP}$ oracle separation of Bouland et al. to exact quantum computation. The separation is based on a variant of the Forrelation problem in which the normalized correlation of one Boolean function with the Fourier transform of another is promised to be exactly $+1/2$ or $-1/2$. The main technical contribution is a repair method that constructs distributions supported on these exact levels while preserving the indistinguishability needed for the $\mathsf{IP}$ and $\mathsf{PH}$ lower bounds. A uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm distinguishes the two cases with certainty using only three oracle queries.

papers.title_en: Succinct Infinite-Horizon Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Are BQP-Complete
papers.abstract_en: Fundamental tasks in linear systems analysis and control require evaluating infinite-horizon output energies for autonomous systems and optimal value functions for controlled systems. These quantities are characterized by Lyapunov and algebraic Riccati equations, respectively. In this work, we study promise problems for their evaluation when the system matrices are sparse and represented succinctly by Boolean circuits specifying their nonzero entries, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. For dissipative autonomous systems with coordinate-vector initial states, we define the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV). Its extension to linear-quadratic optimal control is the succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV). We prove that SLV is $\BQP$-hard: every problem in bounded-error quantum polynomial time ($\BQP$) reduces to it in polynomial time. We then establish that the more general SLQRV problem admits a quantum algorithm running in time polynomial in the succinct input length. Since SLV is a special case of SLQRV, both problems are $\BQP$-complete. Consequently, unless bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time coincides with $\BQP$, no classical randomized algorithm can solve either problem on all promised instances in time polynomial in the succinct input length.

papers.title_en: VNA-Only Calibration of Waveguide Thermistor Mounts with Self-Consistent Determination of the Thermistor-Port Impedance
papers.abstract_en: A method is presented for determining the calibration factor and the effective efficiency of waveguide thermistor mounts from vector-network-analyzer reflection data alone, without a microcalorimeter, extending the three reflection-coefficient method of the coaxial case. In waveguide the thermistor is coupled to the line through a matching structure and the reference impedance of the thermistor port, $Z_0$, is not known a priori; it is inferred through a power-consistency relation between pairs of states, under the convention that it is real. The method reproduces the factory certificates (U = 2 %) of four K486A mounts within 1.0 % rms and the PTB-traceable values (U = 0.85 to 0.98 %) of a fifth within 0.34 % rms; its expanded measurement uncertainty is 0.5 to 1.16 % (k = 2) for the best specimen and below 2 % for the five. A mount with its waveguide-to-coaxial adapter is calibrated directly, without characterizing the adapter, from the model factor of the mount and the geometric factor measured through the adapter. The scattering matrix implied by the solution is not passive; a minimum-norm correction of the thermistor impedances along the two directions invisible to the calibration factor - the ratios of the efficiencies of the three states - brings it to the floor of passivity, where the efficiency depends on the load only through its mismatch factor, leaves the result unchanged, and gives the sensitivity of the efficiency to the bias resistance in closed form: below $4\times10^{-5}$ $Ω^{-1}$ in band mean, proportional to the mismatch of the operating state and to the loss of the mount.

papers.title_en: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
papers.abstract_en: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. We study DQI on random $D$-regular $k$-sparse instances with $k\ge3$, for which local decoders such as belief propagation with quantum messages (BPQM) are commonly used. Such decoders estimate a typical codeword symbol using only the qudits within logarithmic distance of it. Our main insight is that the thresholds of the decoding problem induced by DQI correspond to phase transitions of the Gibbs measure that are well studied in statistical physics: tree reconstruction for local decoders and, for Max-$k$-XORSAT, condensation for the optimal decoder. This insight allows us to prove two main results. First, we prove an information-theoretic obstruction: no local decoder can recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold. Conversely, we show that a decoder based on BPQM reaches this threshold. Since the cavity method predicts that local Markov chains equilibrate rapidly up to the same threshold, we expect DQI with local decoders to give no exponential speedup for sampling and no advantage in approximate optimization with amplitude functions that depend only on the number of violated constraints. Second, we consider the optimal decoder (the pretty-good measurement, for which no efficient implementation is known) and show that it succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold. The condensation threshold thus provides a tight upper bound on the performance of DQI with these amplitude functions, providing a strict refinement of the limit that Jordan et al. derived from the Holevo bound. Our results point to efficient nonlocal decoders that succeed between the two thresholds as the only viable path to a quantum advantage with DQI on these instances.

papers.title_en: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
papers.abstract_en: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

papers.title_en: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
papers.abstract_en: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

papers.title_en: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
papers.abstract_en: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

papers.title_en: The wave equation and two-electron atomic wavefunctions
papers.abstract_en: Axisymmetric solutions of the classical wave equation in three spatial dimensions are shown to be in one-to-one correspondence to functions which annihilate the two-electron kinetic energy operator expressed in coordinates relative to a fixed nucleus.

papers.title_en: Theory overview on LLP searches at the LHC
papers.abstract_en: In these proceedings, we discuss heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) as well-motivated long-lived particle (LLP) candidates to illustrate the rich phenomenology that LLP searches can probe at the LHC. We briefly discuss the minimal HNL scenario, in which the phenomenology is governed by active-sterile neutrino mixing, and its characteristic displaced signatures. We then consider more general BSM scenarios with additional HNL interactions, showing how these can modify the main production and decay mechanisms, opening up new signatures beyond those of the minimal benchmark.

papers.title_en: Reconstruction of pion polarizabilities in lattice QCD with machine learning
papers.abstract_en: We apply the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) from generative machine learning to a model-independent reconstruction of electric and magnetic polarizabilities of both charged and neutral pions. The inputs are the sparse momentum-space four-point-function data in lattice QCD for the connected quark-line contributions obtained in previous simulations at four pion masses between approximately 370 and 1100 MeV on quenched Wilson lattices. For charged pions, the elastic contribution is obtained from the pion form-factor slope, and the complete electric and magnetic inelastic terms are reconstructed separately. The neutral-pion electric and magnetic channels are reconstructed without an elastic charge-radius contribution. Four distinct families of synthetic training functions are employed, so that no single analytic fitting function is prescribed for the lattice data. We present low-momentum reconstructions to the limit of zero momentum transfer where the polarizabilities are defined, and mass extrapolations to the physical pion mass of 138 MeV.

papers.title_en: Multi-TeV vector dark matter in the $U(1)_X$ Higgs portal model
papers.abstract_en: We investigate heavy-mass vector dark matter within the framework of the $U(1)_X$ gauge Higgs portal vector model, by jointly integrating experimental constraints from relic density measurements, direct detection searches, and indirect detection observations alongside the perturbative criterion to derive bounds on the model parameter space. Within the weakly interacting massive particle scenario, we assess the relative contributions of $s$-channel and $t/u$-channel processes to thermal dark matter annihilation. For parameter configurations lying in the $s$-channel resonance region, each fixed value of the scalar mixing angle $\sinα$ corresponds to a well-defined upper limit on the heavy dark scalar mass $m_{h_2}$. This upper limit decreases monotonically with increasing $\sinα$, with a critical threshold of $\sinα\lesssim 0.05$ beyond which perturbative constraints entirely exclude the full resonance corridor. By contrast, the non-resonant parameter regime dominated by $t/u$-channel annihilation processes is found to be excluded for $m_V \simeq 1$ TeV and above under the combined joint constraints from relic density requirements and perturbative consistency. Our results indicate that the perturbative consistency of the scalar sector, enforced via the two-loop renormalisation group equations, imposes bounds on the parameter space in the heavy mass regime that are comparable to, and in some benchmark regions more restrictive than, current experimental limits. Nevertheless, even under the application of these stringent perturbativity constraints, the model still admits a viable set of parameter points spanning a broad multi-TeV mass range.

papers.title_en: Field-induced phase-matching in Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers
papers.abstract_en: Superconducting Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) enable broadband, quantum-limited amplification of weak microwave signals. JTWPAs are essential for the single-shot readout of superconducting qubits, broadband vacuum squeezing, or the generation of microwave cluster states. Phase-matching between signal and pump modes in such JTWPAs represents a major engineering challenge, which is typically solved by integrating resonators in a nonlinear medium in order to tailor electromagnetic dispersion relations and achieve a broadband, high-gain amplification. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a phase-matching approach using a homogeneous nonlinear medium based on Josephson elements by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity. We show how the latter may lead to the sign reversal of the 3-wave mixing nonlinearity and stabilization of the parametric amplification. We envision this technique as a viable alternative to conventional phase-matching approaches.

papers.title_en: Kinematic Quantum Geometry
papers.abstract_en: Kinematic quantum geometry describes fast degrees of freedom (DOFs) that adiabatically follow states parametrized by both the coordinates and the velocities of slow DOFs. It extends Born-Oppenheimer geometry, which depends on coordinates alone, introduces mixed Berry curvatures, and modifies the effective theory governing the slow DOFs. We test its predictions in two setups: spinful particles moving in magnetic textures, and Dirac electrons in graphene coupled to an LC circuit. In the first, kinematic quantum geometry produces a velocity-dependent effective mass tensor and generates a Lorentz-like force nonlinear in velocity that can arise even in coplanar textures. In the second, it renormalizes the circuit capacitance and generates a Hall current nonlinear in the electric field. For small velocities, it reproduces recent results for electronic dynamics in external electromagnetic fields and in pseudospin textures. However, the framework can remain valid at large velocities beyond the perturbative regime, provided the kinematic states are sufficiently slowly varying.

papers.title_en: Frustration-free control for quantum-state preparation: an exact first-passage theory
papers.abstract_en: Quantum circuits based on local measurements and feedback can autonomously prepare and stabilize entangled many-body states. In frustration-free control, the target manifold is specified by local constraints, whose violations are detected by measurement and removed by feedback. We develop an exact theory of this mechanism for the preparation of Dicke states of $N_q$ qubits. Dicke states span the permutation-symmetric subspace, one per magnetization sector. Local singlet projectors define the constraints and detect departures from permutation symmetry. The resulting dynamics closes exactly on the span of the $N_q(N_q-1)/2$ singlet-pair projectors and is equivalent to a classical first-passage process: measurements move the pair endpoints, while feedback absorbs pairs on measured bonds. The closure reduces the exponentially large many-body Liouvillian to a generator of polynomial size. In one dimension we solve this process in closed form. Its slowest rate, $2[1-\cos(π/N_q)]$ in units of the measurement rate, is an exact Liouvillian eigenvalue. For any scheme of this class, the relaxation time is bounded below by the inverse fraction of pair configurations on which feedback acts; local feedback reaches $O(N_q)$ of $O(N_q^2)$ configurations, requiring a time at least linear in $N_q$. A second exact closure determines the final state reached from any initial condition. Extensions to modified transport, restricted feedback, and physical errors yield an exact transport-to-absorber crossover, geometric preparation laws, and a bound on the stationary leakage. An exact second-moment closure determines the ensemble fluctuations: the measurement noise is conserving, while feedback generates removal shot noise and pair correlations. Preparation, acceleration, robustness, and fluctuations are thus governed by one exactly solvable process: the transport and absorption of local constraint violations.

papers.title_en: Long-range correlated quantum errors from diffuson-correlated dephasing
papers.abstract_en: Electrical solid-state qubits are generally initialized, manipulated and read out through diffusive conductors. We show that the disorder-induced low energy modes of such a conductor --- diffusons --- impose spatially correlated dephasing on any qubits that share it, a mechanism we term diffuson-correlated dephasing. Starting from a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model for the disordered conductive region, coupled capacitively to two-level systems, we obtain the noise kernel in closed form. It decays as the inverse square of the qubit separation and changes sign with the orientation of the pair, so that qubit pairs at equal separation may be correlated or anticorrelated, an unambiguous experimental signature. In two dimensions, the correlated noise a single qubit shares with the rest of the array, in the worst-case scenario, grows logarithmically with array size rather than converging. The sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise is therefore violated, so standard threshold theorems no longer guarantee protection against this channel for large qubit arrays. As this dephasing originates from the soft-mode content of the environment rather than on any specific gate detail, we expect correlated dephasing channels of this kind wherever solid-state qubits or sensors share a gapless conductive medium.

papers.title_en: FusionQ: A Generic and Optimal Decoding Framework for Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
papers.abstract_en: Quantum error correction (QEC) decoding has traditionally been organized around fixed decoding instances: a monolithic space-time detector error model (DEM), or a predetermined temporal window, is handed to a backend decoder after enough syndrome data has arrived. This paper presents FusionQ, a fusion decoding framework that changes this paradigm by deriving local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome and then fusing their results into a single global correction. Instead of forcing every shot through the same global or windowed problem, FusionQ builds open-boundary local DEMs around fired detector clusters and expands the corresponding footprints only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors. FusionQ is generic in the decoder backend: the scheduler requires only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, so exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders can share the same runtime. We prove a compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local decoding results yields a global most-likely error (MLE) solution of the original DEM. Our evaluation shows that, with an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot. Across decoder backends, FusionQ substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.

papers.title_en: Long(itudinal) live the helioscope: novel bounds on solar dark photons from conversion on reflecting surfaces
papers.abstract_en: Conventional helioscope searches are insensitive to the longitudinal component of the solar dark photon (DP) flux, which dominates the solar emission for DP masses $m\lesssim 1\,$eV. In this paper, we demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome: using the interface conditions that follow from Maxwell's equations in the presence of a dark photon, we show that a relativistic longitudinal DP flux impinging on a telescope mirror produces an outgoing photon flux. We apply this principle to X-ray helioscopes which employ grazing incidence mirrors. As our main result, we find that BabyIAXO would be competitive with the current world-leading constraints from XENON1T if it can keep sensitivity down to energies of $10\,$eV. Both IAXO and a proposed upgraded version would be able to reach a factor of $\sim 2.5$ and $\sim 13$ deeper than BabyIAXO, respectively, and thus probe a large fraction of unexplored parameter space for $10^{-5}\,\text{eV}\lesssim m\lesssim 0.75\,$eV.

papers.title_en: Finite Measured Entropy Production Does Not Imply Finite Microscopic Irreversibility
papers.abstract_en: Coarse-grained measurements provide a lower bound on entropy production, but how much microscopic irreversibility can they conceal? We construct a driven quantum system in which an imperfect counter registers a finite, strictly positive arrow of time while the microscopic entropy production is infinite. The system is a degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold, coupled to a thermal reservoir through repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas. The oscillator sustains a finite, positive heat current into the vacuum bath, where absorption is forbidden and forward and reverse trajectory laws have different supports. A photon counter with finite collection efficiency, gated time bins, and independent dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of the aligned trajectory laws. For fixed observation duration $\mathcal T$ and detector parameters, we prove that the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as the bath temperature $T_b$ vanishes and is strictly positive at vacuum. The hidden contribution obeys $Σ_{\mathrm{hid}}(\mathcal T,T_b)=\mathcal T\dot Q_0/(k_BT_b)+O(1)$, where $\dot Q_0>0$ is the stationary vacuum heat current. False positives conceal the support mismatch while preserving measurable time asymmetry. Thus, finite and informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility.

papers.title_en: AlphaHits: Full-Event Tracking and Reconstruction Towards a Hit-Level Foundation Model
papers.abstract_en: We introduce AlphaHits, a Transformer-based approach towards hit-level foundation models for LHC physics, building on the TrackFormer and HiggsFormer architectures. AlphaHits operates directly on detector hits and demonstrates scalable full-event charged-particle reconstruction and multi-task event reconstruction and classification from low-level detector information. AlphaHits-TrackFormer reconstructs the full charged-particle content of complete TrackML events without imposing a transverse-momentum selection on the target tracks. It processes both pixel and strip hits in events containing up to $1.5\times10^5$ hits under HL-LHC-like pileup conditions and assigns hits to individual reconstructed trajectories across its kinematic range. This includes the challenging low-$p_T$ population down to approximately $150\,\mathrm{MeV}$ in TrackML samples. It achieves a TrackML score of 0.959 over all reconstructable tracks, representing, to our knowledge, the highest reported TrackML score for full-detector, inclusive charged-particle reconstruction. Building on the TrackFormer architecture, AlphaHits is pretrained on charged-particle tracking and fine-tuned for multi-task reconstruction and classification. From a shared hit-level representation, it predicts tracks, jets, jet flavour, and event-level observables. AlphaHits achieves an AUC of 0.944 for Higgs event classification, with performance comparable to a Particle Transformer (ParT) baseline using fully reconstructed inputs. It also achieves performance comparable to Delphes-based baselines for jet reconstruction, jet flavour classification, and missing transverse momentum regression. These results highlight the potential for scalable full-event tracking and multi-task learning directly from detector hits, representing a promising step towards transferable hit-level representations and general-purpose foundation models for LHC physics.

papers.title_en: Which data samples matter when training a quantum model?
papers.abstract_en: The expressivity, loss landscapes, and generalization behavior of quantum machine learning models have been studied extensively, yet mainly from a model-centric point of view. Little is known about the compatibility of particular quantum models with specific datasets. In this work, we study quantum machine learning models with a data-dependent focus by establishing a quantum-compatible form of the V-usable information. This metric quantifies the information a model can extract from a dataset, enabling a direct, data-centric comparison of different models. We employ this metric to study which data points contribute most significantly to a model's learning process. This enables us to develop an informed preselection strategy for data subsets that can significantly improve the data efficiency of the training pipeline. This work establishes the V-usable information as a powerful diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and a practical route to data-efficient quantum machine learning.

papers.title_en: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits
papers.abstract_en: Quantum processors now measure qubits in the middle of a circuit, and the stream of outcomes is the raw output of error correction, measurement-based state preparation and monitored dynamics. For a scrambling circuit, predicting the statistics of this stream is as hard as simulating the processor, so there is no exact reference to check it against once the device outgrows classical simulation. We show that near the light cone the problem becomes exactly solvable, for any two-qubit gate. In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, measurements along the edge of the light cone form a two-state Markov chain, and measurements $d$ sites inside the edge are generated by $\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1$ qubits that move with it, while the rest of the chain, however large, acts on them as a memoryless bath. The memory of the record is therefore quantized, one bit on the edge and at most one more for every site of displacement, a bound that generic gates attain. The same causal structure determines which hardware noise the record can see, removes that sensitivity at no gate cost, and yields a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, a demonstration with its analysis specified in advance finds the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone, and none where the theory forbids it. This gives dynamic circuits an exact reference at any system size, and shows that the collision models of open-system theory arise exactly inside chaotic dynamics.

papers.title_en: Third-Order Quantum Information from Distributed Randomized Measurements
papers.abstract_en: Randomized measurements offer a way to probe nonlinear properties of quantum states without reconstructing their full density matrices. For states shared between distant laboratories, we study products of three outcome probabilities measured at the same local settings and then averaged over independent local random unitaries. We determine, for an arbitrary number of parties, which third-order local-unitary invariant combinations these averages retain and which they cannot separate. The accessible information is encoded in algebraic invariants of the quantum state and is reconstructed by analysing the permutation symmetries induced by the distributed measurement protocol. Exploiting these symmetries, the reconstruction problem collapses, regardless of the number of measurement outcomes, to the symbolic inversion of a 3 x 3 matrix. As a result, nonlinear information can be extracted without inverting the exponentially large matrices that typically arise in distributed multipartite quantum systems.

papers.title_en: Quantum Control Geometry as a Metric of Chaos
papers.abstract_en: Quantum-chaotic systems share the same coarse-grained features characteristic of random matrices, such as Wigner-Dyson level-spacing statistics, yet can exhibit strikingly different eigenstate structure and many-body dynamics, including relaxation, transport, scrambling, and entanglement growth. This raises the fundamental question of whether these finer-grained features probe genuinely distinct aspects of quantum chaos or, instead, reflect different manifestations of a common underlying structure---and whether such structure provides a meaningful basis for regarding one many-body quantum system as "more chaotic" than another. Here, we address this question by introducing a quantum geometric framework that quantifies the susceptibility of many-body eigenstates to physically allowed deformations of the Hamiltonian, as constrained by spatial locality, symmetries, and conservation laws. The resulting geometric susceptibility is quantitative, providing a metric of chaos beyond traditional binary diagnostics; intrinsic, as it depends on the manifold of allowed Hamiltonian deformations rather than on the way the system is probed; and unifying, as it directly connects eigenstate structure with dynamics. For canonical models of quantum chaos, we find that minimal geometric susceptibility, maximal eigenstate randomness, broad spectral response of local operators, and the suppression of nonhydrodynamic slow structure coalesce in the same region of Hamiltonian control space. This suggests that these seemingly distinct signatures of chaos are different manifestations of a common underlying geometric structure. Our framework provides a route toward understanding the limits of relaxation and scrambling under physical constraints; in applications, it offers a means to engineer strongly chaotic regimes in programmable quantum systems with restricted controls.

papers.title_en: Early State Exclusion for $5\times5$ Jacobi Matrices
papers.abstract_en: In this paper, we present a problem that arose from quantum computing, when the quantum state to be transferred completely vanishes before the first occurrence of the perfect state transfer. It was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with $n$ of qubits, where $n>4$ is an odd number. We present the solution for $n=5$. The proofs are accessible to students who studied trigonometry and calculus. As for the set-up the knowledge of eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra is needed.

papers.title_en: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
papers.abstract_en: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

papers.title_en: Dynamics of Rényi entanglement entropies and Eigenstate Thermalization
papers.abstract_en: How is entanglement dynamics encoded in the eigenstates of the time-evolution operator? We address this question by focusing on Rényi entropy dynamics in deterministic chaotic Floquet models in arbitrary dimensions. Inspired by the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), we employ spectral representations of reduced density matrix moments (purity and its higher-order generalizations) whose decay through spectral dephasing captures nonequilibrium entanglement growth. These representations closely resemble those governing local-observable dynamics, but involve eigenstates in a replicated Hilbert space and observables are replaced by subsystem permutation operators, such as the swap operator for Rényi-2. Focusing on Rényi-2, we combine exact random matrix theory calculations, established ETH results and numerical tests in 1D to formulate ETH-like ansätze for subsystem swap matrix elements in the replicated eigenbasis and their cross-correlations with initial-state overlap statistics. In the thermodynamic limit, purity dynamics is entirely determined by smooth slowly varying functions that emerge from such statistics, paralleling generalized ETH formulations in a single replica. In the limit of large subsystems, these functions exhibit a striking structural simplification: locality of the dynamics together with bulk spectral dephasing reduce their functional dependence to a single fundamental frequency. Our formalism provides a setting where ETH-like statements naturally coexist for both arbitrarily small and large subsystem sizes. We discuss extensions of our results to higher Rényi entropies. Beyond clarifying the spectral foundations of entanglement dynamics, these results lay some of the groundwork for future applications of spectral filter methods to the computation of Rényi evolution in deterministic systems.

papers.title_en: Exceptional points in non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion: From coefficient dynamics to state signatures
papers.abstract_en: An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form $O$ operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.

papers.title_en: Syndrome extraction for quantum LDPC codes in silicon: Distributed entanglement and mobile ancillas
papers.abstract_en: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 $μ$m and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about $4$-$5\times10^{-4}$, roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.

papers.title_en: Rational quantum spectral filtering by repeat-until-success protocol
papers.abstract_en: We introduce a finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework for implementing rational spectral filters on a quantum computer, extending spectral filtering beyond the polynomial transformations implemented by quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). Our approach interleaves queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator $X$, whose spectrum lies in $[-1,1]$, and mid-circuit measurements that either accept, reject, or continue the computation without resetting the quantum state. Although the protocol may run for arbitrarily many rounds, its terminal statistics are determined by a finite-dimensional Lyapunov equation. Under uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry, we characterize exactly the spectral filters $R(X)$ realizable upon acceptance: $R$ can be any real rational function with no poles on $[-1,1]$ and values in $[0,1]$. We provide a constructive compiler for any admissible $R$, with bounds on memory and expected query cost, and characterize the accepted quantum operation through a spectral coherence kernel. Applications to regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy yield exact low-degree realizations and query-cost advantages over the fixed-depth QSVT polynomial-postselection baseline considered here, with all repetitions and independent restarts after rejection included in the cost.

papers.title_en: PriorTilt: Decoding quantum LDPC codes with sparse perturbations of belief propagation priors
papers.abstract_en: Although belief propagation (BP) is a widely adopted decoder for classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, its accuracy is limited in the quantum setting. We introduce \PriorTilt, a variant of BP obtained by selectively perturbing a small fraction of its prior log-likelihood ratios using offsets determined by recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, while preserving the same message-passing rules. We compare \PriorTilt with Relay-BP and beam search decoders for circuit-level decoding of three benchmark codes. \PriorTilt achieves a lower logical error rate (LER) than both baselines at every tested data point. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ Gross code BB144 at noise rate $p=10^{-3}$, the LER reductions reach $4.3\times$ relative to Relay-BP and $3.1\times$ relative to the beam search decoder. At $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt has lower mean decoding times than Relay-BP on all three codes and achieves mean decoding speedups of approximately $2.6\times$--$3.0\times$ over the beam search decoder. For BB144 at $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt achieves an LER approximately $610\times$ lower than the standard min-sum BP decoder with the same iteration budget, while perturbing fewer than $0.5\%$ of its priors per round on average.

papers.title_en: The Alpha Clustering Model of the EMC Effect
papers.abstract_en: For more than forty years, the EMC effect, the observation that nuclear structure functions in deep-inelastic scattering appear to be modified relative to the free-nucleon expectation, has resisted a consensus microscopic explanation. In this letter, we argue that the strength and $A$ dependence of the EMC effect may be governed by the phenomena of $α$ clustering in nuclei and responsible for a majority of the partonic modification associated with the EMC Effect. We motivate the alpha clustering model of the EMC effect (ACME), and with a data driven approach, we demonstrate how such a model can reproduce the existing deep inelastic scattering data on nuclei. We make predictions for other nuclei such as $^{16}$O, $^{20}$Ne, and $^{48}$Ca and explore its consequences for a spin-dependent EMC effect and global analysis of nuclear parton distributions.

papers.title_en: A Two-Component Pressure Model for Casimir Forces With Implications for Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant
papers.abstract_en: <jats:p>A phenomenological two-component pressure model is presented for the Casimir effect and its extension to dark energy and the cosmological constant. The interaction between closely spaced plates is described as a balance between an effective background compressive pressure associated with underlying oscillatory dynamics and a short-range repulsive contribution arising from matter-induced effects. Within this formulation, the characteristic inverse fourth-power dependence of the Casimir force is reproduced, with consistency achieved with experimentally observed trends. The framework is extended to larger scales by treating the compressive component as a uniform background pressure and by introducing a matter-induced dark-energy contribution within the intervening region. In this context, the cosmological constant is interpreted as the net pressure arising from the difference between the background compressive contribution and the repulsive component and is associated with an effective large-scale energy density. Numerical analysis and illustrative plots demonstrate that the evolution of the scale factor is governed by the sign of the net pressure. A critical density is identified that separates expanding and contracting regimes: negative net pressure leads to accelerated expansion, whereas positive net pressure results in contraction. Although the formulation is phenomenological and not intended as a first-principles derivation, it provides a consistent pressure-based framework linking confined interactions with large-scale dynamical behavior.</jats:p>

papers.title_en: Impact of multi-dot configurations on electron temperature and double quantum dot latching in gate-controlled qubit devices
papers.abstract_en: Many currently envisaged scalable architectures for Si/SiGe spin qubit devices utilize gate-controlled multi-dot configurations characterized by their peculiar Coulomb blockade physics. One example is the concurrent use of a single electron transistor (SET) as a charge sensor and as a reservoir for adjacent qubit quantum dots (QD). We find that the SET energy spectrum impacts pulsed gate spectroscopy of the QD when the SET simultaneously acts as the reservoir and the sensor. Then, using the qubit QD as a probe, we quantify how strongly the electron temperature of the SET depends on the applied bias. It surpasses a reference experiment by 100 $mK$ even at 50 $μV$ bias. Our results provide a strong incentive for choosing spin qubit initialization schemes which do not rely on coupling to the reservoir in such devices. Switching to a double quantum dot connected to a single reservoir, a frequent configuration for qubit readout, we finally demonstrate the tunability of the characteristic latching behavior by systematically mapping it in the few-electron stability diagram.

papers.title_en: Quantum-enhanced hybrid optical gyroscope with two-mode squeezed states
papers.abstract_en: Quantum resources promise to surpass classical limits in measurement precision, enabling sensors to reach ultimate sensitivity bounds. In conventional optical gyroscopes using laser probes, the angular velocity sensitivity is fundamentally constrained by the shot-noise limit. Here, we propose a hybrid nonlinear-linear optical gyroscope that integrates both nonlinear and linear interferometric elements to achieve sensitivity enhancements beyond this classical limit. We theoretically analyze the performance of the proposed scheme under various input seeding conditions and evaluate its robustness against realistic experimental imperfections, including photon losses and detection inefficiency for two different intensity detection schemes, i.e., intensity sum and intensity difference. Our results demonstrate that the gyroscope configuration is resilient to inefficient detection; even in the presence of photon losses, the coherent seeded configurations show significant quantum enhancement. Specifically, with <math><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> photon loss in every optical path and <math><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> detection inefficiency in intensity-difference measurement, the proposed configuration with a coherent seed input yields 9 dB of quantum enhancement in sensitivity beyond the classical limit when probed with two-mode squeezed states with 13 dB of squeezing. These findings suggest that hybrid nonlinear-linear optical gyroscopes provide a robust pathway for the realization of quantum-enhanced navigation and inertial sensing.

papers.title_en: Delivery of refractory radioactive ion beams via in-trap decay at ISOLDE
papers.abstract_en: An approach to deliver intense ion beams of refractory radioactive isotopes utilizing in-trap <math><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></math> decay is demonstrated using the gas-filled ISCOOL ion trap at CERN-ISOLDE. Ion beams of <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rb</mi><none/><mo>+</mo><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>97</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>98</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></math> and <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Sr</mi><none/><mo>+</mo><mprescripts/><none/><mn>98</mn></mmultiscripts></math> were injected into the ion trap, where they underwent <math><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></math> decay and the daughter ions were successfully confined in the same trap. The produced singly charged ions were subsequently extracted and identified using the ISOLTRAP multireflection time-of-flight mass spectrometer, where the beam composition was analyzed as a function of trapping time. Modeling the observed time-dependent populations of the parent and daughter ions using the Bateman equations reproduces the isotopes' known half-lives, thereby confirming production via in-trap decay, achieving an overall efficiency for the singly charged daughter beams on the order of <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> relative to the parent intensity. Using this method, delivery of a singly charged atomic ion beam of <math><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi><none/><mo>+</mo><mprescripts/><none/><mn>98</mn></mmultiscripts></math> is thus reported for the first time at ISOLDE. These results demonstrate a practical and operationally simple method for delivering refractory isotopes at thick-target isotope-separation-on-line facilities, opening new opportunities for nuclear-structure studies of chemically challenging isotopes.

papers.title_en: Evolution of collectivity near <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow></math>: Lifetime and electromagnetic transition strengths of the first excited <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></math> state in <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Ga</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>69</mn></mmultiscripts></math> from <math><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mtext>-</mtext><mi>γ</mi></mrow></math> fast-timing measurements
papers.abstract_en: The low-spin structure of the odd-proton nucleus <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Ga</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>69</mn></mmultiscripts></math> (<math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>38</mn></mrow></math>) near <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow></math> has been investigated through a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches. The lifetime of the first excited state <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></math> has been measured for the first time using the <math><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mtext>-</mtext><mi>γ</mi></mrow></math> fast-timing technique with picosecond resolution, yielding a mean lifetime of <math><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>106</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> ps, equivalent to a half-life of <math><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>73</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> ps, from which the reduced transition probabilities <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>E</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> for the <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>→</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></math> (ground state) transition have been extracted. Large-scale shell-model calculations employing the GX1APN and JUN45PN effective interactions have been performed for the odd-<math><mi>A</mi></math> Ga isotopes with <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>34</mn></mrow></math> to 40 for comparison. The systematic comparison of transition strengths across the odd-<math><mi>A</mi></math> Ga isotopic chain, supported by large-scale shell-model calculations, is consistent with a gradual structural change from a collectively mixed proton-neutron configuration toward a more single-particle-dominated structure as <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow></math> is approached.

papers.title_en: Configuration-constrained multiquasiparticle states in <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>–</mo><mn>152</mn></mrow></math> Fm–Sg isotones
papers.abstract_en: Configuration-constrained potential-energy-surface calculations are performed for two- and four-quasiparticle states in the eight even-even <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>152</mn></mrow></math> Fm–Sg isotones using a deformed Woods-Saxon potential, Lipkin-Nogami pairing, and Strutinsky macroscopic-microscopic energies. Vacuum and blocked surfaces are minimized independently over deformations <math><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>. Orbital-overlap tracing preserves the blocked Nilsson configurations near avoided crossings, while component decompositions and species-dependent pairing-gap reductions provide complementary validation. Across the two isotonic chains, the neutron <math><msup><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></math> and <math><msup><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></math> excitations increase from <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow></math> to <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>152</mn></mrow></math>, whereas the neutron <math><msup><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></math> sequence decreases. The proton <math><msup><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></math> sequence develops a pronounced minimum near Rf, with calculated energies of 1.120 and 1.123 MeV in <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rf</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>254</mn></mmultiscripts></math> and <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rf</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>256</mn></mmultiscripts></math>. All minima remain strongly deformed, with <math><mrow><mn>0.231</mn><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.251</mn></mrow></math>, small <math><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></math>, and predominantly negative, configuration-dependent <math><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>6</mn></msub></math>. Blocking produces only small shape polarization, although the <math><msubsup><mn>16</mn><mn>613</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup></math> and <math><msubsup><mn>16</mn><mn>624</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup></math> families show slightly different nonaxial responses. In <math><mmultiscripts><mi>No</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>254</mn></mmultiscripts></math>, the <math><msup><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></math> bandhead is reproduced within 30 keV, whereas the neutron <math><msup><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></math> state is underestimated by 0.534 MeV despite retaining the intended <math><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mn>734</mn><mo>]</mo></mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></math> and <math><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mn>725</mn><mo>]</mo></mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></math> orbital character. The sensitivity to the neutron pairing strength is examined: its 10% increase reproduces the empirical pairing indicator but leaves the <math><msup><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></math> energy 0.346 MeV below experiment, implicating the <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>152</mn></mrow></math> single-particle spacing and possibly residual correlations. The calculated <math><msubsup><mn>16</mn><mn>613</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup></math> state at 2.737 MeV lies closer to the experimental 2.933-MeV <math><msup><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></math> state than the <math><msubsup><mn>16</mn><mn>624</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup></math> solution at 3.749 MeV, favoring the <math><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mn>613</mn><mo>]</mo></mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math> configuration at the uncorrected mean-field level.

papers.title_en: Lifetime measurements in <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rh</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>95</mn></mmultiscripts></math> and <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Ru</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>95</mn></mmultiscripts></math>: Investigation of seniority conservation in the <math><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math> isotones
papers.abstract_en: Excited states in <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rh</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>95</mn></mmultiscripts></math> and <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Ru</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>95</mn></mmultiscripts></math> have been populated in fusion-evaporation reactions and their lifetimes have been measured using the fast-timing technique with a setup consisting of LaBr scintillators and high-purity germanium detectors. The resulting lifetimes are used to calculate reduced quadrupole transition probabilities and discussed within the context of seniority conservation in the <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> orbital. In contrast to the latest experimental findings, the new experimental data indicate that seniority symmetry is partially conserved in the midshell nucleus <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Rh</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>95</mn></mmultiscripts></math>.

papers.title_en: Microscopic mechanism underlying charge-radius trends in Fayans pairing
papers.abstract_en: The Fayans energy density functional (EDF), and in particular its pairing sector, has been claimed to be able to reproduce the experimental data of charge radii in many instances. A particularly intriguing case is that of the <math><mi>Ca</mi></math> isotopes between <math><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow></math> and 48, where charge radii exhibit a “bell shape.” In our work, we examine the microscopic origin of this behavior. The pairing part of the Fayans EDF contains three essential parameters: the overall strength <math><mi>f</mi></math> and the density-dependent and density-gradient terms, <math><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>̃</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math> and <math><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>̃</mo></mover><mtext>D</mtext></msub></math>. We select a number of parametrizations, fixing the overall strength <math><mi>f</mi></math> to reproduce the pairing gap of <math><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>Ca</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mrow><mn>44</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow></math>. We find that some parameter sets enhance the charge radii in open-shell nuclei and reproduce the bell shape of the charge radii of <math><mi>Ca</mi></math> isotopes. It is found that this effect originates from the repulsive nature of the rearrangement potential, and cannot be mocked up by a refit of the pairing strength. On the other hand, none of the parametrizations that we have considered can reproduce satisfactorily the experimental charge radii of <math><mi>Ca</mi><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>Sn</mi></math>, and <math><mi>Pb</mi></math> isotopes at the same time.

papers.title_en: Deformed nuclei; how to separate the wheat from the chaff
papers.abstract_en: The quadrupole-quadrupole correlations are dominant in all nuclei with neutrons and protons outside magic closures. A subset among these shows features reminiscent of semiclassical rotors, i.e. J(J+1) spectra, and spectroscopic quadrupole moments and transition probabilities B(E2)'s consistent with the Bohr-Mottelson ansatz. But in the great majority of the cases the situation is not so clear. The Kumar-Cline invariants are an invaluable tool to decide to what extent the shape parameters $\beta $ and $\gamma $ are meaningful.

papers.title_en: The quantum Euclid algorithm and its application to factoring
papers.abstract_en: We present a quantum implementation of the Euclid algorithm for calculating the Greatest Common Divisor when one of the integers involved is a compound of two odd-valued primes. We discuss a possible application to the quantum factoring problem, for which modular exponentiation is no longer required, and the factors are revealed directly by measurements, although the method does not scale for large numbers in a favourable manner.

papers.title_en: Quantum neural networks for wind power prediction: a benchmark against classical machine learning models
papers.abstract_en: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) are frequently proposed for regression on small datasets, yet the design and evaluation choices that govern their accuracy are rarely isolated. This study benchmarks six QNN circuits, built from a Z feature map and a real-amplitudes ansatz with six entanglement strategies and each trained with two readout scalings, against 11 classical regressors, including gradient boosting, support vector regression, and recurrent and attention-based networks, for predicting wind turbine power from four meteorological measurements. Because consecutive samples are strongly autocorrelated, all models are evaluated by blocked cross-validation with buffers, and conventional random cross-validation is analyzed for comparison. The readout scaling has the largest effect: mapping the target to [0, 1] instead of $[-1, 1]$ lowers the test error of every configuration by 39-46%, and the best configuration, with circular entanglement, reaches $R^2$ of 0.88-0.89 with 12 trainable parameters. The best QNN selected by validation significantly outperforms linear regression and k-nearest neighbors and trails support vector regression, a decision tree, and XGBoost by 16-40  kW, while LightGBM and the neural networks remain ahead ($R^2$ of 0.92-0.93). The ordering of the entangling gates alone changes the error by up to 17%, and the time per objective evaluation grows linearly with the training size and increases with the gate count. Random cross-validation overstates accuracy most strongly for k-nearest neighbors and for QNNs with the $[-1, 1]$ readout.

papers.title_en: Metrological channels induced by encrypted quantum cloning: Optimal-probe Fisher-information broadcasting and single-use operational recovery
papers.abstract_en: Encrypted quantum cloning creates multiple individually inaccessible signal systems from which an unknown input state can be recovered by combining any selected signal with a shared quantum key. Here we study parameter estimation when a local sensing transformation is applied after encrypted cloning and before decryption. For the two-clone qubit protocol, a local Pauli rotation on one encrypted signal is shown to induce, after standard decryption, a parameter-dependent Pauli dephasing channel rather than a unitary rotation. We derive its Pauli-transfer representation and the corresponding quantum Fisher information (QFI) for arbitrary mixed qubit probes. We then distinguish raw QFI, which for an optimal decoded probe may remain simultaneously present in a decoded output and its complement, from decoder-accessible QFI, which is operationally single-use because a first decryption destroys the shared syndrome information needed for a second standard recovery. For <math><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> encrypted clones, the effective channel family is independent of clone number up to a clone-parity-dependent permutation of the Pauli axes (the single-clone case is exceptional for <math><mi>Y</mi></math> sensing, where the decoded map stays unitary). This produces a metrological parity switch: For fixed probe and generator, even and odd clone numbers can yield respectively vanishing and maximal QFI. Closed expressions are obtained for the degradation of this parity contrast under probe depolarization and Pauli-diagonal Bloch-vector contraction.

papers.title_en: Quantum reduction for lattice-based cryptanalysis: VQA framework for Bounded Distance Decoding
papers.abstract_en: Bounded Distance Decoding (BDD) is an essential problem in post-quantum cryptography. This work presents a Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) framework that directly encodes BDD on q-ary lattices as the Hamiltonian ground state, avoiding conventional reduction to Shortest Vector Problem (SVP). Thanks to this direct encoding, we can build a non-degenerate cost function, reduce its dimension, and lower qubit requirements for NISQ-era VQAs. This framework can be applied to cryptanalytic targets-such as Learning with Errors (LWE) with side-channel hints and NTRU-designing specialized Hamiltonians that exploit problem structure and small-secret properties. In typical parameter regimes, our approach-by directly encoding BDD as a Hamiltonian ground state and avoiding the SVP reduction-reduces qubit requirements by 36.4-74.1% (Lindner-Peikert 36.4-43.1%, Regev 66.8-74.1%) relative to Joseph et al. and by 5.8-49.2% (Lindner-Peikert 5.8-24.2%, Regev 35.3-49.2%) relative to Albrecht et al. Our method provides a complexity estimator and validates our analysis through numerical simulations, demonstrating that VQA-based cryptanalysis is a quantifiable, complementary threat vector for post-quantum security evaluation.

papers.title_en: Solution Size Growth as an Obstacle to Iterative Refinement for Linear Optimization
papers.abstract_en: Iterative refinement is a technique used to exponentially boost the precision of the solution to certain problems by solving a sequence of related problem instances. We study the size of the solutions arising from the sequence of problems produced by the iterative refinement algorithm when applied to linear optimization problems (LPs). We introduce a class of problems for which the size of such solutions can grow exponentially with the number of refinement iterations, and we show evidence that to avoid this undesirable behavior, a black-box LP solver would have to be \emph{lucky}---a concept introduced formally in this paper, by which we mean that the solver would have to return a solution of better quality than what is required by its termination tolerances.
